passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Ageing Populations and Pension Systems

A Ageing populations shift the ratio of retirees to workers, pressuring pay-as-you-go pension systems funded by current contributions rather than fully capitalised reserves. Demographic transition theory links lower fertility and longer life expectancy to greying societies across East Asia, Europe, and Latin America. Policymakers raise statutory retirement ages, yet manual labourers in hazardous occupations resist uniform delays citing unequal health spans. The author argues intergenerational contracts must be renegotiated transparently to avoid portraying elders as burdens rather than contributors with accumulated skills and unpaid caregiving histories. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

B Defined-benefit public schemes promise formula-based pensions, while defined-contribution plans shift investment risk to individuals navigating volatile markets. Chilean-style privatisation experiments produced mixed results after fee drag and crisis losses, prompting partial reversions toward public solidarity tiers. Notional defined contribution systems track earnings profiles without literal individual accounts, blending predictability with demographic indexing. Actuarial projections depend on migration inflows supplementing workforces, though anti-immigrant politics can undermine remedies demographers recommend for shrinking contributor bases in rural regions losing youth to cities. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

C Gender inequalities appear because women interrupt careers for care work, lowering lifetime contributions and survivor benefits in two-earner rules favouring highest earners. Divorced partners may lack equitable splits without explicit pension credit sharing for childrearing years. Widowhood poverty persists where benefits tie to deceased husbands' records in legacy structures being reformed slowly. Feminist economists advocate caregiver credits and minimum guarantees decoupled from paid employment intensity, arguing justice requires recognising reproductive labour underpinning future taxpayers who will fund tomorrow's retirees under any sustainable formula. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

D Health spending accelerates as multimorbidity clusters in late life, competing with pension outlays in consolidated fiscal frameworks. Long-term care insurance proposals spread catastrophic costs of nursing home years, yet moral hazard and means-testing dilemmas complicate design. Ageing in place policies adapt housing with grab bars and community nurses, cheaper than institutional beds when support networks exist. Without preventative chronic disease management, medical inflation will consume savings meant for modest retirement consumption, worsening inequality between elders with affluent children and those relying solely on public transfers at subsistence levels. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

E Employers adapt workplaces with ergonomic adjustments and phased retirement bridging part-time roles to mentorship, retaining tacit knowledge while reducing full salary loads. Age discrimination nonetheless pushes older job seekers toward gig platforms lacking pension contributions. Unions negotiate supplemental occupational pensions now often converted to lump sums at job change, tempting members to spend rather than annuitise. Financial literacy campaigns promote compound growth for youth, arriving too late for cohorts nearing retirement with inadequate balances after decades of wage stagnation and housing costs consuming disposable income needed for voluntary savings top-ups. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

F Political coalitions fragment: young taxpayers resist financing generous elder benefits they doubt will reciprocate when they retire, while pensioner lobbies mobilise high turnout to defend indexation formulas linking payments to wage growth or prices. Constitutional courts strike reforms deemed retroactive takings of accrued rights, forcing gradual parametric adjustments. International organisations publish sustainability indices ranking countries by projected replacement rates, naming automatic stabilisers like longevity indexing that slow benefit growth as life expectancy rises without sudden cliff-edge cuts provoking street protests seen in capital cities during austerity decades. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

G Looking ahead, the author envisions multi-pillar systems blending modest public floors, employer savings, and family solidarity realistic about demographic facts. Delaying retirement alone is insufficient without lifelong learning and health equity. If societies fail to value care work and migration contributions, pension crises will manifest as elder poverty rather than abstract fiscal gaps. Proactive communication about trade-offs, paired with anti-discrimination enforcement and affordable care, offers a more cohesive social contract than panic cuts that pit generations against each other in electoral cycles fueled by demographic anxiety narratives. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.
